## Part 1 · 00:01

[00:01] One of the most common atheist arguments is that religion causes wars. Historical analysis shows that this claim is exaggerated. Out of all recorded human wars, only about 7% were primarily caused by religion. If Islamic conflicts are removed from that number, it drops closer to 3%. The vast majority of wars have been fought over political power, territory, resources, or ethnic rivalries. While religion has at times been misused as a justification for violence, it is not the dominant driver of war in human history.

[00:33] Another frequent objection is that a lot of evil has been done in the name of religion. This is true, but it cannot be used as proof that religion itself is false. For example, individuals such as Stalin, Mao, and Paul Pot who rejected religion entirely were responsible for some of the deadliest regimes in history. The point is not that atheism is to blame for their crimes, but rather that human evil can manifest under both religious and secular systems. Using the misdeeds of some believers to discredit the truth of belief itself is a category error.

[01:04] Atheists also argue that if someone were born in another country, they would not be a Christian. While cultural background does influence what people believe, this reasoning applies equally to atheism. An atheist born in a strongly religious culture would likely not hold the same views either. Context shapes beliefs, but it does not decide which worldview is true. The real question remains, which explanation of reality best fits the evidence of human existence, morality, and the universe itself. Another argument is the claim, how do you know which religion is true?

[01:35] This question assumes that the existence of many faiths discredits the truth of any single one, but everyone, whether religious or not, holds a worldview that they place faith in. Some worldviews are labeled religious and others are considered secular, but each one requires a foundation of trust in unseen truths. The task is to examine which worldview best explains the origin of the universe, the reality of moral law, the presence of consciousness, and the purpose of life. Another common claim is that there's no scientific proof that God exists.

[02:08] This argument misunderstands both science and God. Science by definition studies the natural world. Things that can be measured, tested, and observed. God by definition exists beyond the natural world. That means science cannot prove or disprove God in the same way it cannot scientifically prove concepts like human rights, moral truths, or the existence of love. These are real, but they belong to categories outside the limits of laboratory testing. Some insist there is no evidence of anything supernatural.

[02:40] Yet history and medical documentation point to cases that strongly challenge a purely naturalistic worldview. Reports of demonic possession include individuals speaking languages they never learned or demonstrating knowledge they had no access to. Near-death experiences also show people acquiring verified information while unconscious or clinically dead. These accounts may be debated, but they cannot be dismissed as if there were no evidence at all. Another objection is that the Bible has contradictions. This argument assumes that supposed inconsistencies in scripture prove it unreliable.

[03:06] But for 2,000 years, theologians and scholars have examined and explained these apparent conflicts. Often, what looks like a contradiction is clarified by context, differences in perspective, or translation issues. For example, the four gospels highlight different details of the same events, much like multiple eyewitnesses would. Variation in detail does not equal contradiction but can actually strengthen the reliability of the overall record. Atheists also argue that the gospels were anonymous implying we do not know who wrote them.

[03:42] In reality, anonymity in ancient writings does not mean total uncertainty of authorship. Early church fathers who lived close to the time of the apostles recorded who wrote the gospels and their testimony consistently matches the traditional attributions of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The absence of a signature in the text itself does not negate the strong historical evidence for their authorship. Another objection is that the gospels misquote Jesus. Some secular scholars argue that parts of the gospels are a blend of authentic sayings from Jesus and later editions by the early church.

[04:12] The difficulty is that these same scholars cannot agree on which sayings are genuine and which are not. Because of this lack of consensus, their claims cannot carry decisive weight. The gospels have been preserved and transmitted with extraordinary care. And the church fathers who knew the apostles affirmed their accuracy. A frequent argument is that Jesus never claimed to be God. While Jesus did not walk around saying the exact words, "I am God, worship me," his actions and teachings revealed his divine identity.

[04:46] In all four gospels, Jesus does things that only God can do, such as forgiving sins, calming storms by command, and receiving worship. He often challenged his followers with the question, "Who do you say that I am?" which forced them to recognize his true nature. After his resurrection, his disciples openly confessed him as God, and Jesus affirmed their faith. Another claim is that the later a gospel was written, the more divine Jesus appears, suggesting that his godhood was a later invention. This theory collapses when considering the letters of Paul.

[05:15] These writings predate the gospels and already present a clear confession of Jesus as divine. For instance, in Philippians chapter 2, Paul describes Jesus as existing in the form of God before taking on human nature. Since this belief was present from the very earliest writings, it cannot be explained as a gradual invention over time. Critics also point to slavery in the Bible as proof that scripture condones oppression. However, the presence of slavery in the biblical text is not the same as approval of it.

[05:46] In the Old Testament, certain laws address slavery within the context of the ancient world, often regulating and restricting practices rather than endorsing them. Jesus explained that some Old Testament laws were accommodations to human hardness of heart. Furthermore, Christian influence was the primary force behind the eventual abolition of slavery. In fact, abolitionist movements in both Europe and America were overwhelmingly led by Christians. One common objection is that God killed many people in the Bible. Scripture does record judgments where God ends lives.

[06:13] But the Bible also teaches that God is the giver of life and numbers every person's days. Because God is the author of life, he has the authority to take it. These judgments are portrayed as responses to sin and corruption, not arbitrary acts. The idea of divine judgment is uncomfortable, but it is tied to the concept of divine justice. That sin brings consequences and God has the right to administer them. Another argument is that atheist countries are more prosperous. It is true that some modern secular nations such as those in Northern Europe are prosperous and stable.

[06:46] However, correlation is not causation. Prosperity often weakens a society's sense of dependence on God, leading to secularization rather than atheism causing prosperity. Furthermore, these nations became prosperous while deeply rooted in Christian values and culture for centuries. In contrast, countries such as communist China, built explicitly on atheistic ideology, show how rejection of God does not guarantee freedom or prosperity. Atheists sometimes argue that since there are thousands of gods in human history, rejecting one more god, the Christian God, makes sense.

[07:22] But this is a false comparison. The question of whether any god exists is entirely different from the question of which religion best describes him. Dismissing all gods is not the same as thoughtfully considering evidence for the existence of a creator. If God exists and is the cause of all reality, then the existence of many false gods does not cancel out the reality of the true one. Another frequent challenge is the question, if God created everything, who created God? This misunderstands what Christians mean by God?

[07:56] By definition, God is the uncaused cause, the necessary being who exists outside of time and matter. Everything in the universe has a beginning, but the chain of causes cannot stretch backward into infinity. There must be a first cause, and the Christian claim is that this cause is a personal God who intentionally brought the universe into being. Some claim that science disproves God. Historically, this is false. The church was central in the development of modern science. Many of the founders of the scientific revolution such as Galileo, Kepler, and Newton were devout believers in God.

[08:25] Medieval theologians laid the intellectual foundation by teaching that the universe is orderly because it was created by an intelligent creator. This belief gave scientists confidence that the natural world could be studied and understood. Far from disproving God, science arose from the conviction that God's creation is rational. Another objection is that God is only used to fill in the gaps where science has no explanation. This idea is called the God of the gaps. Christianity does not claim that God is simply a placeholder for the unknown.

[08:56] Instead, God is the ultimate explanation for everything, including what science already explains. Science describes the how of natural processes, but God provides the why. For example, science can describe how gravity functions, but it cannot explain why a universe exists with such precise physical laws in the first place. Atheists sometimes ask, "If God is good, why does he not destroy evil right now?" The Christian answer is that he eventually will, but if he did so immediately, he would also have to remove every human being who sins.

[09:28] God delays judgment out of mercy, giving people time to repent. A related question is why God allows suffering, including the suffering of animals that do not sin. Scripture teaches that all creation is fallen, but also promises restoration. The hope is that God will ultimately redeem and compensate all that has suffered. Another challenge is the suggestion that perhaps God himself is evil. This collapses under logical examination. Evil is not an independent substance, but the absence of good, just as darkness is the absence of light.

[09:59] For good to be objective, it must have a source greater than human opinion. If God did not exist, objective good and evil would not exist either. A God who is objectively evil is impossible because evil can only exist as a lack of good, not as a foundation in itself. A familiar challenge is the question, can God make a rock so heavy that he cannot lift it? This is a logical trick rather than a real objection. Being all powerful does not mean that God can perform contradictions or act against his own nature. For example, God cannot lie, cease to exist, or create another God.

## Part 2 · 10:31

[10:31] Omnipotence refers to God's power over creation, not to self-contradictory actions. The rock question is therefore meaningless. It describes an impossible situation, not a genuine limit on divine power. Another objection asks why God allowed evil to exist at all. According to Christian teaching, the reason is that a greater good comes through God's victory over evil. Triumphing over sin, death, and Satan brings greater glory than if evil had never existed. This framework means that evil is temporary and serves as a backdrop for the revelation of God's justice, mercy, and power.

[11:06] Some argue that religion is just wishful thinking. If that were true, one would expect religious texts to focus on comfort and positivity. The Bible, however, emphasizes human sinfulness, brokenness, and need for repentance. Hardly the message people would invent if they were only seeking comfort. Its central figure, Jesus, was rejected and crucified, not celebrated as a worldly hero. The difficulty of its message points away from it being mere wishful invention. Psychology is often used to explain away belief in God.

[11:39] The claim is that human beings created the idea of God because it fulfills emotional or social needs. But if God is real, it is natural to expect that believing in him would bring psychological benefits since he designed human beings to find fulfillment in relationship with him. In the same way, the fact that food satisfies hunger does not mean that hunger invented food. Psychological explanations do not disprove the reality of what is believed in. Some argue that spiritual experiences can be explained entirely by brain chemistry, but this reasoning is flawed.

[12:09] Romantic love also produces measurable chemical reactions in the brain. Yet, no one concludes that spouses or partners are imaginary. The existence of brain activity during an experience does not prove that the experience has no external cause. If God is real, it is reasonable that encounters with him would affect the human brain in ways that can be measured. Others claim that druginduced hallucinations prove spiritual experiences are only brain-based. Yet, people who have had both drug trips and near-death experiences consistently report that the two are completely different.

[12:40] Drug hallucinations are chaotic, distorted, and fleeting, while near-death experiences are described as clear, coherent, and life-changing. The quality and consistency of these testimonies suggests that not all altered states of consciousness can be reduced to chemical illusions. A popular internet claim is that the story of Jesus was copied from the story of Horus or other mythological figures. This idea has been widely circulated on forums and in videos, but is rejected even by secular scholars.

[13:15] Detailed comparison shows that the supposed parallels between Jesus and pagan gods are either fabricated or extremely superficial. The historical evidence is clear that the accounts of Jesus's life arose in first century Judea, not from recycled pagan myths. Another frequent objection is that faith is the opposite of logic and reason. In reality, faith means trust. People exercise faith in everyday life. When eating food without scientifically proving it is safe, or when trusting that a spouse truly loves them.

[13:43] Faith is not blind belief without evidence, but reasonable trust based on knowledge and experience. In Christianity, faith is trust in God's character, promises, and revealed truth. One objection is that evolution proves God did not create the world. This argument assumes that evolution and creation are mutually exclusive. In fact, throughout church history, many Christian thinkers have allowed for natural processes as part of God's creative work. Long before Charles Darwin, some theologians interpreted the opening chapters of Genesis in a more figurative or symbolic way.

[14:13] The Christian position is not restricted to one view of how life developed, but affirms that God is ultimately the source and sustainer of all creation, whether through direct acts or natural processes. Another claim is that Christianity only spread through military conquest. Historical records contradict this. For its first 300 years, Christianity was illegal within the Roman Empire, and believers often faced severe persecution. Yet the faith grew rapidly, not through violence, but through its compelling message and the witness of those willing to suffer for their belief.

[14:43] By the time Constantine legalized Christianity, it was already widespread, having convinced people across the empire despite harsh opposition. A related argument is that Constantine invented what we now call Christianity. This is a myth. The central beliefs of Christianity such as the divinity of Jesus, his death and resurrection, and salvation by faith were firmly established and widely practiced long before Constantine's reign. His role was political. He ended persecution and gave Christianity official recognition.

[15:18] The substance of the faith was not invented by him, but rooted in the teachings of Jesus and the apostles from the very beginning. Another objection is that the existence of many Christian denominations proves the religion is not true. While it is correct that Christianity has divided into different groups, the disagreements are mostly about secondary issues such as worship style, church structure, or interpretation of certain doctrines.

[15:49] On the core truths such as the belief in one God, the divinity of Jesus, his death and resurrection, and salvation through him, there is overwhelming unity across denominations. The variety of traditions does not erase the central agreement on the essentials of the faith. Some argue that there is no evidence for Jesus outside the Bible. This claim is inaccurate. Non-Christian sources from the first century mention him. The Jewish historian Josephus wrote about Jesus in his antiquities of the Jews. The Roman historian Tacitus also referred to Jesus and his execution under Pontius Pilate.

[16:12] These references, though brief, confirm that Jesus was a historical figure recognized even by those outside the Christian faith. Because of this, nearly all modern scholars, whether religious or not, accept that Jesus truly existed. A final objection is that the universe is far too vast for God to care about individual human beings. With billions of galaxies and stars, it can seem unlikely that human life is significant. However, size does not determine value. A single human soul can have greater worth than an entire planet of lifeless matter.

[16:46] Christian teaching holds that God created the vastness of the universe not to diminish human importance but to display his glory. At the same time, scripture emphasizes that this same God knows every detail of his creation, even numbering the hairs on each person's head. But if you think atheist arguments are challenging, wait until you see the lives of the men who walked with Jesus. Each disciple carried a story that shaped the faith we know today. Don't miss it.
